task.prompt: You can designate only a few strategic accounts. Rank these by strategic value, highest first.

items.label: One-off client: $20,000 project, no further plans
Healthcare platform: $250,000 a year, growing, 35% margin, strong champion, will act as a reference
Fintech scale-up: $90,000 a year, three business units not yet served, 40% margin
Retail chain: $600,000 a year, 12% margin after rate cuts, planning to move work offshore

task.explanation: Strategic value combines growth potential, profitability and relationship strength, not just current revenue. A big account with low margin and plans to leave needs a plan, but it is not where future value lies.

prompt: Find the weaknesses in this strategic account plan.

task.prompt: Mark the lines in this strategic account plan that are weak.

segments.text: Client goal for the year: reduce cost-to-serve by 15% through automation.
Our goal: double revenue from the account.
segments.issue: Our goal is not linked to the client's goal; growth should come from helping them reach theirs.

segments.text: Relationship map: CIO (sponsor), CFO (budget), two directors (users).
Whitespace: claims, billing and customer-support units not yet served.

segments.issue: Every strategic account has risks; list them (champion changes, competitors, budget cuts).

segments.text: Executive sponsor on our side: to be decided.
segments.issue: Strategic accounts need a named senior sponsor on your side.

segments.text: Quarterly business review dates agreed for the year.

task.prompt: Account A: revenue $600,000, delivery cost $528,000, account management cost $30,000. Account B: revenue $250,000, delivery cost $162,500, account management cost $15,000.

fields.label: Account A contribution after account management
Account B contribution after account management

task.explanation: A: margin = 72,000 ÷ 600,000 = 12%; contribution = $42000. B: contribution = $72500 on less than half the revenue. Size is not the same as value.

prompt: Respond to a volume rate-cut request from a strategic account.

task.prompt: Your largest account asks for a 15% rate cut "because of our volume". Your margin on the account is already 18%.

steps.question: What is your first move?
options: Cut the rate and quietly reduce seniority on the team
Show the account's economics and explore trades such as longer commitments, a blended team, or scope changes
steps.explanation: A 15% cut would nearly wipe out an 18% margin; trade on structure, and never reduce quality covertly.

steps.question: They agree to a two-year commitment. What can you offer?
options: A smaller rate reduction tied to the commitment and guaranteed volume
A one-off discount without any commitment
steps.explanation: Price follows risk: committed volume justifies some movement.

prompt: Decide how many strategic accounts to run.

task.prompt: Your team of three account managers wants to label 20 accounts as strategic.

steps.question: What do you advise?
options: Make the 20 largest by revenue strategic
Limit it to the few accounts that justify deep investment, based on agreed criteria
steps.explanation: Strategic status means heavier investment; spreading it across many accounts dilutes it.

steps.question: Which criteria should drive the choice?
options: Which clients are easiest to talk to
Growth potential, profitability, relationship strength and strategic fit
steps.explanation: Balanced criteria stop the biggest but least profitable accounts from crowding out better ones.

prompt: Estimate whitespace in a strategic account.

task.prompt: You serve one business unit of a client at $200,000 a year. Three other units each have an estimated $150,000 a year of relevant work. You estimate a 30% chance of winning each within 18 months.

fields.label: Total whitespace across the three units

task.explanation: Total = 3 × 150,000 = $450,000. Weighted = 450,000 × 0.3 = $135000. Whitespace analysis shows where to focus relationship-building next.

prompt: What is the purpose of a strategic account plan?

options: To align your growth in the account with the client's own goals over 1–3 years
To set the client's internal budget
mcq.explanation: A good plan starts from the client's goals and maps how you help reach them.

prompt: Your strategic account's revenue is high but margin has dropped to 10% after repeated rate cuts. What is the best approach?

options: Keep accepting cuts to protect revenue
Review the account economics openly with the client and restructure the engagement
mcq.explanation: Revenue at very thin margin is risky; restructuring (scope, team mix, commitments) is better than silent erosion.

prompt: Why should a strategic account have an executive sponsor on your side?

options: To build senior relationships and unblock decisions that the account manager cannot
mcq.explanation: Executive-to-executive relationships give strategic accounts resilience and access.
